structure.rationale: The 14-chapter order comes from the requester's syllabus (issue #187) and is kept as given. It runs from the running database (architecture, undo/redo, multitenant), through building and securing the environment, to protecting data and recovering, then observing and tuning, and finally changing and keeping it available. Each part relies on vocabulary from the one before; the order of the later chapters follows the syllabus. Baseline release: Oracle Database 19c, a long-term release still widely run in production, with Premier Support reported through 2029 and Extended Support through 2032. 23ai has been renamed 26ai, and its Extended Support date was not yet announced when checked. Version-specific and licensing-dependent features (e.g. AWR/ASH under the Diagnostics Pack) are flagged per chapter. Each chapter follows the notes' shape: problem, mechanism, tools, worked example, lab, injected failure, remediation, validation/rollback, checklist, with one running order-processing case study. The book is narrated in the Thing Explainer persona, so real terms appear once in quotes beside a plain description.
structure.audience: Readers who already know SQL, relational databases and basic transactions, and want to run Oracle in production; SQL fundamentals and installation walkthroughs are out of scope.

claims.text: A database is the set of files on disk (datafiles, control files, online redo logs); an instance is the memory (SGA) plus background processes that opens and serves it.

The SGA is shared memory holding the database buffer cache, shared pool (including library cache), redo log buffer and more; each server process also has private PGA memory (e.g. sort and hash work areas).

SQL processing runs parse, execute, fetch (fetch for queries). A soft parse reuses a cursor already in the library cache; a hard parse builds a new plan and is costlier. Bind variables let statements share cursors.
Server processes read blocks into the buffer cache; changes are made to cached blocks (making them dirty) and generate redo and undo; the change is not written to datafiles at that moment.

Changes are first described in the redo log buffer. On COMMIT, LGWR writes the buffer to the online redo log; the commit completes (the session waits on 'log file sync') once that write is done. DBWn writes dirty blocks later and lazily.
LGWR also writes when the buffer is a third full, every ~3 seconds, and before DBWn writes dirty blocks (write-ahead logging); concurrent commits can share one write (group commit).
Checkpoints (CKPT) advance a checkpoint position recorded in the control file and datafile headers; DBWn writes dirty blocks to move it forward. Checkpoint also happens at log switch.

Instance recovery after a crash is done automatically by SMON/at open: roll forward by applying redo from the checkpoint position to the end of the log (cache recovery), then roll back uncommitted transactions using undo (transaction recovery). Committed data survives because its redo reached disk.

Online redo log groups are written in a circular fashion; a group cannot be reused until its changes are checkpointed (and archived, if in ARCHIVELOG mode). Multiplexing members across disks guards against losing one copy.

The control file records the database name, datafile and redo log locations, checkpoint info and backup metadata; it is read at MOUNT. Startup stages: NOMOUNT (instance), MOUNT (control file), OPEN (datafiles and redo).
Dedicated server mode gives each session its own server process; shared server mode uses dispatchers and a pool. Main background processes: PMON/PMAN, SMON, DBWn, LGWR, CKPT, ARCn.
Useful views: V$INSTANCE, V$DATABASE, V$SGAINFO, V$PROCESS, V$SESSION, V$LOG, V$LOGFILE, V$CONTROLFILE, V$DATAFILE, V$SYSSTAT, V$SESSTAT, V$SQL, V$LOG_HISTORY.

snippets.code:
SELECT instance_name, status, database_status FROM v$instance;
SELECT name, log_mode, open_mode FROM v$database;

SELECT group#, sequence#, status, members FROM v$log;
SELECT group#, member FROM v$logfile;

SELECT n.name, s.value FROM v$mystat s JOIN v$statname n USING (statistic#)
WHERE n.name IN ('redo size','user commits','session logical reads');

ALTER SYSTEM CHECKPOINT;
ALTER SYSTEM SWITCH LOGFILE;
snippets.note: lab only; do not run at busy times in production

pitfalls: Believing COMMIT writes data blocks to datafiles; it writes redo.
Calling the instance the database (or the reverse) when tracing a fault.
Sizing redo logs so small that log switches and checkpoints come every few seconds.
Treating 'log file sync' waits as a DBWn problem; they point at LGWR and redo disk latency.
Forcing checkpoints or log switches in production 'to be safe'.

claims.text: The System Change Number (SCN) is a database-wide logical clock that increases with each commit; Oracle stamps changes and read snapshots with SCNs to order events.

Undo records how to reverse a change and serves read consistency, rollback and recovery of uncommitted work; redo records how to re-make a change and serves roll-forward recovery. A change generates both; undo is itself protected by redo.
Readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers: a query sees data as of its snapshot SCN, rebuilding older block versions by applying undo to a copy of the block (consistent read).

Default read consistency is statement-level: each query sees data as of the SCN at its start. Transaction-level consistency needs SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY or ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE (the latter can raise ORA-08177). READ COMMITTED is the default isolation level.

Row locks are taken by INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE/SELECT FOR UPDATE and held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK. The transaction also takes a TX enqueue lock; a session wanting a locked row waits on that TX lock (wait event 'enq: TX - row lock contention'). Oracle has no lock escalation.

Blocking is found with V$SESSION (BLOCKING_SESSION, FINAL_BLOCKING_SESSION, WAIT_CLASS/EVENT, SQL_ID) and V$LOCK (TYPE, LMODE, REQUEST). Killing the blocker is ALTER SYSTEM KILL SESSION 'sid,serial#' and rolls back its work, which can itself take time.

Deadlock: two sessions each hold a row the other wants. Oracle detects it, rolls back the statement of one session (not the whole transaction), raises ORA-00060 and writes a trace file named in the alert log. The application must handle it. Common avoidable cause: unindexed foreign keys and inconsistent lock order.

With automatic undo management, undo lives in an undo tablespace. Active (uncommitted) undo is never overwritten; unexpired undo (committed, younger than retention) is kept if space allows; expired undo is reused first. UNDO_RETENTION is a target in seconds, not a guarantee, unless the tablespace has RETENTION GUARANTEE (which can make DML fail with ORA-30036 when undo is full).

ORA-01555 'snapshot too old' occurs when a query needs undo that has been overwritten, so it cannot rebuild the block as of its snapshot. Causes: queries running longer than undo covers, undo too small for the change rate, or frequent commits reusing undo; also delayed block cleanout and fetching across commits. Fixes: tune the query, raise undo size/UNDO_RETENTION, avoid committing inside the loop that is reading.

V$UNDOSTAT keeps ten-minute rows with UNDOBLKS, TXNCOUNT, MAXQUERYLEN (longest query in seconds), MAXQUERYID, SSOLDERRCNT (ORA-01555 count) and NOSPACEERRCNT; with auto-tuned retention, TUNED_UNDORETENTION shows the retention in effect. The alert log records ORA-01555 with the SQL ID.
Flashback Query (SELECT ... AS OF TIMESTAMP/SCN) uses the same undo; how far back it reaches depends on undo retention.
Instance recovery uses redo to roll forward then undo to roll back uncommitted transactions; this ties this chapter to the previous one.

snippets.code:
SELECT CURRENT_SCN FROM v$database;
SELECT dbms_flashback.get_system_change_number FROM dual;
snippets.note: 19c; the latter needs EXECUTE on DBMS_FLASHBACK

snippets.code:
SELECT sid, serial#, blocking_session, final_blocking_session, event, seconds_in_wait, sql_id
FROM v$session WHERE blocking_session IS NOT NULL;

SELECT begin_time, undoblks, txncount, maxquerylen, ssolderrcnt, nospaceerrcnt, tuned_undoretention
FROM v$undostat ORDER BY begin_time DESC FETCH FIRST 12 ROWS ONLY;

SELECT tablespace_name, retention FROM dba_tablespaces WHERE contents='UNDO';
SHOW PARAMETER undo
SELECT status, SUM(bytes)/1024/1024 mb FROM dba_undo_extents GROUP BY status;

pitfalls: Thinking COMMIT frequency is free: committing inside a loop that reads the same table invites ORA-01555 and breaks atomicity.
Believing readers wait for writers (true in many other databases, not Oracle).
Setting UNDO_RETENTION huge without sizing the undo tablespace.
Killing the blocking session without checking what it was doing; its rollback may take as long as its work did.
Treating deadlock ORA-00060 as an Oracle bug; the application's lock order is the cause.
Using RETENTION GUARANTEE casually: it can make writers fail instead of readers.
Conflating undo (reverse) with redo (replay).

claims.text: A multitenant container database (CDB) holds one root (CDB$ROOT, CON_ID 1), one seed PDB (PDB$SEED, CON_ID 2, read-only template) and zero or more pluggable databases (PDBs). One instance (one SGA, one set of background processes, shared redo and control files) serves all containers.

Each PDB has its own data dictionary for its own objects, its own SYSTEM/SYSAUX and application tablespaces and datafiles, and its own temp; metadata for Oracle-supplied objects lives in the root and is linked.
Application containers (12.2+) are a special PDB kind: an application root plus application PDBs that share application-owned common objects. Not the same as ordinary user PDBs.

Common users exist in all containers and are created in the root; common user names must start with C## (or the value of COMMON_USER_PREFIX) unless Oracle-supplied. Local users exist in one PDB only and cannot be created in the root. A privilege granted locally applies only in that container; granted with CONTAINER=ALL from the root it applies in all.
ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER=<name> moves a session with proper privileges between root and PDBs without reconnecting; SHOW CON_NAME or SYS_CONTEXT('USERENV','CON_NAME') reports the current container.

Each PDB gets a default service with the PDB's name that the listener registers; clients should connect to a PDB through its service name, not a SID. Extra services can be added per PDB (e.g. DBMS_SERVICE or srvctl).

After a CDB restart, PDBs are left MOUNTED unless their state was saved with ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE ... SAVE STATE (available since 12.1.0.2). Opening: ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE name OPEN; closing: CLOSE IMMEDIATE.

CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE from the seed needs an ADMIN USER clause; that user becomes a local administrator in the new PDB. FILE_NAME_CONVERT (or Oracle Managed Files / CREATE_FILE_DEST) decides where the files go.

CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE new FROM existing clones a PDB. A hot clone (source stays open read write) needs local undo mode and ARCHIVELOG mode; otherwise the source must be open read only. Remote clone uses a database link (FROM pdb@dblink).

Unplug writes an XML manifest (or .pdb archive) describing the PDB: ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE x UNPLUG INTO 'file'; then DROP PLUGGABLE DATABASE x KEEP DATAFILES. Plugging in uses CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE ... USING 'file' with COPY, MOVE or NOCOPY; DBMS_PDB.CHECK_PLUG_COMPATIBILITY checks compatibility first; PDB_PLUG_IN_VIOLATIONS records mismatches.

Views: V$CONTAINERS, V$PDBS, CDB_PDBS (list containers); CDB_* dictionary views show data for all containers when queried from the root, while DBA_* views show only the current container. Most V$ views have a CON_ID column.

Parameters: most initialization parameters are CDB-wide, set in the root; those flagged ISPDB_MODIFIABLE in V$SYSTEM_PARAMETER can be set inside a PDB. ALTER SYSTEM SET ... CONTAINER=ALL|CURRENT scopes the change.

Redo logs, control files and (in shared undo mode) the undo tablespace are CDB-level; in local undo mode each PDB has its own undo tablespace. Backups: RMAN can back up the whole CDB or single PDBs; PDB point-in-time recovery exists. Resource Manager (CDB plans) and per-PDB limits such as MAX_PDB_STORAGE share resources between PDBs.

Licensing: on Enterprise Edition 19c up to three user-created PDBs per CDB are allowed without the Multitenant option; the software does not enforce the count. 12c/18c allowed one. Edition rules for Standard Edition 2 are reported inconsistently by secondary sources; confirm in the Licensing Information manual.
Cloning a PDB into a Data Guard primary can leave the standby without the new PDB's datafiles; Oracle suggests a transient clone with STANDBYS=NONE for such cases.
Non-CDB architecture is deprecated since 12.1 and desupported from 21c; 19c still allows non-CDB.

snippets.code:
SHOW CON_NAME
SELECT con_id, name, open_mode FROM v$pdbs ORDER BY con_id;

snippets.note: paths are examples; omit convert with OMF

snippets.code:
CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE orderstest FROM ordersdev;
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE orderstest OPEN;
snippets.note: source must be read only unless local undo + ARCHIVELOG

snippets.code:
ALTER SESSION SET CONTAINER = orderstest;
SELECT sys_context('USERENV','CON_NAME') FROM dual;

CREATE USER c##ops IDENTIFIED BY "<password>" CONTAINER=ALL;
GRANT CREATE SESSION TO c##ops CONTAINER=ALL;

pitfalls: Running ALTER SYSTEM or a grant in the root and thinking it only touched one PDB (or the reverse).
PDBs left MOUNTED after restart because state was never saved.
Connecting by SID or to the root service when the app needs the PDB service.
Hot clone refused because the CDB is in shared undo mode or NOARCHIVELOG.
Creating a 4th PDB on Enterprise Edition without the Multitenant option; the software won't stop you.
Cloning a production PDB copies production data; mask before giving it to dev.

claims.text: ALTER SYSTEM SET ... SCOPE= takes MEMORY (running instance only, lost at restart), SPFILE (next startup only) or BOTH (default when started with an SPFILE). Static parameters can only use SCOPE=SPFILE.

Startup passes through NOMOUNT (instance: memory and background processes, parameter file read), MOUNT (control file opened) and OPEN (datafiles and redo opened). ALTER SYSTEM is usable from NOMOUNT on.

Shutdown modes: NORMAL waits for all sessions to leave; TRANSACTIONAL waits for open transactions; IMMEDIATE rolls back active transactions and disconnects; ABORT does no cleanup and needs instance recovery at next startup.
An SPFILE can be created from a PFILE (CREATE SPFILE FROM PFILE) and back (CREATE PFILE FROM SPFILE) without starting the instance. The SPFILE is binary and must not be hand-edited.

On Linux, the oracle-database-preinstall-19c package (Oracle Linux/RHEL family) creates the oracle user and oinstall/dba groups and sets kernel parameters and shell limits; practitioner guides show fs.file-max=6815744, aio-max-nr=1048576, nofile and nproc limits for the oracle user.

DBCA can create a database non-interactively with dbca -silent -createDatabase, taking template, gdbname, sid, character set and createAsContainerDatabase options; a response file can hold the same answers.

ORACLE_HOME (the software tree) and ORACLE_SID (the instance name) are environment variables; a DB is bound to the home that created it, so patching strategy depends on the home layout. The database name, instance name and service name are different things.

V$PARAMETER / V$SYSTEM_PARAMETER show running values; V$SPPARAMETER shows what the SPFILE holds; a mismatch is configuration drift between memory and file. ISSYS_MODIFIABLE says IMMEDIATE, DEFERRED or FALSE.
In a CDB, init parameters are set at the CDB level; a PDB may override those marked ISPDB_MODIFIABLE. Multitenant is the only architecture for new databases from 21c.

snippets.code: CREATE PFILE='/stage/init_backup.ora' FROM SPFILE;
dbca -silent -createDatabase -templateName General_Purpose.dbc -gdbname ORCL -sid ORCL -characterSet AL32UTF8 -createAsContainerDatabase true -numberOfPDBs 1 -pdbName orders
snippets.note: passwords supplied via prompt/response file, not shown; verify options with dbca -help

pitfalls: SCOPE=MEMORY change silently vanishes at restart; SCOPE=SPFILE does not take effect now.
Hand-editing init.ora while the instance uses an SPFILE does nothing.
Static parameter set with default SCOPE fails with ORA-02095.
Different ORACLE_HOME or ORACLE_SID in a cron shell than in your login shell.
Passwords typed on a command line show up in process lists and shell history.

claims.text: A client connection goes to a listener (default TCP 1521), which hands it to a service; the client names a service in a connect descriptor (HOST, PORT, SERVICE_NAME).
The listener works with no listener.ora using defaults (TCP 1521); database services register dynamically with it via the LREG process, with no manual listener.ora entries.

LOCAL_LISTENER points registration at a non-default local listener; REMOTE_LISTENER registers with listeners elsewhere. ALTER SYSTEM REGISTER forces registration now. Registration can lag up to about a minute after startup.

Prefer SERVICE_NAME over SID in connect descriptors: services are logical names (a database can have many) and each PDB has its own default service named after the PDB; SID connects only to an instance and cannot reach a PDB.

Name resolution methods: Easy Connect (host:port/service), local naming (tnsnames.ora, found via TNS_ADMIN or $ORACLE_HOME/network/admin), directory naming (LDAP). NAMES.DIRECTORY_PATH in sqlnet.ora sets the order.

Dedicated server: one server process per session. Shared server: dispatchers (DISPATCHERS parameter) pass requests to a pool of shared server processes (SHARED_SERVERS); SERVER=DEDICATED in the descriptor forces a dedicated process. Long-running or admin work should use dedicated.

Diagnostic ladder: lsnrctl status/services on the server shows the listener and registered services; tnsping tests the listener and name resolution only (not authentication or the database); sqlplus user@//host:port/service tests the full path.

ORA-12541 TNS:no listener: nothing is answering at the host:port tried (listener down, wrong port, or blocked). ORA-12514: the listener answered but does not know the requested service. ORA-12154: the name could not be resolved (client naming). ORA-12170: connect timeout, often a firewall dropping packets. ORA-01017: invalid username/password (authentication reached the database).

Native network encryption and integrity are set in sqlnet.ora (SQLNET.ENCRYPTION_SERVER/CLIENT, SQLNET.CRYPTO_CHECKSUM_*), with values ACCEPTED, REJECTED, REQUESTED, REQUIRED; TLS uses the TCPS protocol with a wallet and a TCPS listener endpoint (commonly port 2484 or 1522).

From the database side, connection pools hold many long-lived sessions; a pool bigger than the database's PROCESSES/SESSIONS limit gives ORA-00020 (maximum processes exceeded), and a connection storm (many new logons at once) is a listener and logon cost; the listener rate limit and QUEUESIZE can matter. Sessions are visible in V$SESSION with MACHINE, PROGRAM, SERVICE_NAME.

Local works but remote fails: a local BEQ/bequeath connection (no listener, using ORACLE_SID) bypasses the network entirely; so 'works on the server' proves the database is open and says nothing about the listener, service registration, host firewall or client naming.
A listener binding to 'localhost' or the wrong host name/IP (listener.ora HOST) accepts local but refuses remote connections; check with lsnrctl status and the OS (ss -ltn).

snippets.code:
lsnrctl status
lsnrctl services

tnsping //dbhost:1521/orders_svc
sqlplus app_user@//dbhost:1521/orders_svc
snippets.note: from the application host; Easy Connect syntax host:port/service

snippets.code:
ALTER SYSTEM SET local_listener='(ADDRESS=(PROTOCOL=TCP)(HOST=dbhost)(PORT=1521))' SCOPE=BOTH;
ALTER SYSTEM REGISTER;

ORDERS =
  (DESCRIPTION=
    (ADDRESS=(PROTOCOL=TCP)(HOST=dbhost)(PORT=1521))
    (CONNECT_DATA=(SERVICE_NAME=orders_svc)))

pitfalls: tnsping success does not prove login will work.
Using SID where only a PDB service exists.
Editing the wrong tnsnames.ora: TNS_ADMIN overrides the home's network/admin.
Listener started before the database: services missing until registration catches up; ALTER SYSTEM REGISTER.
Host firewall open on server but a network firewall in between drops packets silently: timeout, not refusal.
Pool max larger than PROCESSES.
